**Title:** OntoCoDec: Type-Constrained Information Extraction via Compiled Schema Constraints

**Abstract:** Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples—where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints. These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present OntoCoDec, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints. A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to ≤0.21% at F1 40–46%, converting irrecoverable type errors to correctable cross-field inconsistencies (CF ≤1.4%); beam search (k=4) eliminates all violation types at 1.39× latency. In zero-shot settings, DR reductions span 76–99% on SciERC and 42–90% on DocRED; CF increases are concentrated in hallucinated entities (58.1%) and decrease with scale and fine-tuning.

\section{Reproducibility Details}
\label{app:reproducibility}

\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
All runs use seed 42.

\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.

\paragraph{Inference time.}
Inference timing is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:runtime} (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, same hardware as training).

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that compiles information extraction ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Evaluated across three 8B-class models and two relation extraction datasets (up to 96 relations), OntoCoDec composed with LoRA fine-tuning reduces domain/range violations to $\leq$\,0.21\% at F1 40--46\%, converting irrecoverable type errors to correctable cross-field inconsistencies (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%); beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 1.39$\times$ latency.
In zero-shot settings, DR reductions span 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED; CF increases are concentrated in hallucinated entities (58.1\%) and decrease with scale and fine-tuning.
\end{abstract}

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) in zero-shot settings; Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B additionally under LoRA fine-tuning, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

INT4 (AWQ) quantization preserves constraint enforcement across both datasets: DR remains at 0\% for all four model--dataset configurations under INT4, with the sole FP16 violation (Llama SciERC, 0.09\%) disappearing after quantization.
R-F1 changes range from $-$2.06 to $+$0.69\,pp, consistent with expected quantization quality costs independent of the constraint layers.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); 97.6--100\% of removed triples are false positives (\S\ref{sec:downstream-impact}). Beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) in zero-shot settings; Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B additionally under LoRA fine-tuning, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).

Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}
